articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Linked to Iranian Missile Program
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions target entities and individuals allegedly involved in Iran's ballistic missile program and its proliferation activities.

The designations aim to disrupt networks supporting Iran's military capabilities and its regional proxies. This move is part of ongoing U.S. efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities in the Middle East and beyond.
Further details regarding the specific entities and individuals designated, as well as the implications for those engaging with them, are available on the Treasury website.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Sanctions on Cyber Actors, Criminal Organizations, and Cuba-Related Entities
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related malicious actors, transnational criminal organizations, and entities connected to Cuba.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating cybercrime, disrupting illicit financial networks, and addressing human rights concerns in Cuba. The actions aim to prevent these actors from accessing the U.S. financial system.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also published a Cuba-related determination, providing further guidance on the scope and implementation of the new measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of a broader strategy to exert pressure on the Iranian regime.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an Iran-related alert to inform the public about potential risks and compliance obligations. The agency also published an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question, providing updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.
These measures reflect the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy, with continuous adjustments made to address evolving geopolitical landscapes and illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. The specifics of this amended license are crucial for individuals and entities engaged in activities permitted under the updated guidance.
Stakeholders are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals Linked to North Korea and DRC
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The North Korea designations aim to counter the regime's weapons of mass destruction programs and illicit revenue generation. The DRC-related designations address human rights abuses and corruption within the region.
These actions underscore the U.S. commitment to promoting human rights, stability, and non-proliferation globally through targeted sanctions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

Details of the settlement, including the specific violations and the agreed-upon penalty, are outlined in the official agreement. This action highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.
Companies are reminded of the importance of robust compliance programs to prevent and detect potential sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: On October 26, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These updated FAQs provide clarification and guidance on critical compliance procedures for financial institutions and other entities subject to OFAC regulations. The amendments aim to enhance understanding and facilitate adherence to reporting requirements.
Compliance professionals should review these updated FAQs to ensure their internal procedures align with the latest OFAC guidance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new General Licenses related to Iran and Russia, providing authorizations for certain transactions.

In a separate action, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. These removals indicate a reassessment of sanctions targets based on evolving circumstances.
Additionally, amended Frequently Asked Questions were issued concerning Iran and Russia, offering further clarity on the scope of the new General Licenses and other related policies.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: On October 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target entities and individuals involved in intellectual property theft.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses to authorize certain activities that might otherwise be prohibited. These licenses aim to minimize unintended consequences while upholding the integrity of the PAIPA sanctions program.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to protecting American intellectual property and combating economic espionage.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026. This update provides further guidance on transactions involving Venezuela.

The amended General License modifies existing authorizations, and the new FAQ offers additional clarity on specific aspects of the Venezuela sanctions program. These adjustments reflect ongoing policy considerations regarding the situation in Venezuela.
Entities engaging in Venezuela-related activities should review these updates to ensure compliance with the latest regulatory framework.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined Over $1.5 Million by OFAC
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $1,529,685 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 27, 2026. This penalty is a result of apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding companies accountable for sanctions compliance failures. Companies are urged to implement robust compliance programs to prevent such violations.
The specific details of the violations leading to this penalty are outlined in the enforcement information released by OFAC.

articles.headline: Bank of America Hit with Over $11.6 Million OFAC Penalty
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026. This significant penalty stems from apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This OFAC penalty is part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included a $1.2 billion fine from FinCEN and a $750 million civil monetary penalty from the OCC for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.

The enforcement actions highlight the critical importance of comprehensive and effective sanctions and AML compliance programs for financial institutions, particularly those with extensive global operations.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined Over $175,000 by OFAC
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $175,015 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 9, 2026. The penalty is for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
This enforcement action serves as a reminder to logistics and shipping companies of their obligations to comply with U.S. sanctions laws and to implement appropriate screening mechanisms.
The details of the violations leading to this penalty are available in the enforcement information published by OFAC.

articles.headline: Individual Assessed Over $1.4 Million OFAC Penalty
body: An individual has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026. This penalty is for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

This enforcement action highlights that OFAC pursues violations by individuals as well as corporate entities. Individuals involved in international transactions are responsible for ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.
Further details regarding the nature of the violations and the identity of the individual are available in the public enforcement information.

articles.headline: OCC Announces October 2026 Enforcement Actions Against Banks and Individuals
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, targeting both financial institutions and institution-affiliated parties. These actions are designed to correct deficient practices and violations.

Key actions include a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, including failures in suspicious activity reporting and customer due diligence.

Additionally, a $750 million civil money penalty was assessed against Bank of America, National Association, for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and issues with inaccurate transmittor name information in wire transfers.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.
